lessons.title: Move it to where it belongs
lessons.hook: One column parked in the wrong table, and every edit means chasing down every copy.

blocks.heading: Ask what a column actually depends on
blocks.body: Every table should describe one kind of thing, keyed by one thing. If a column's value depends on only part of a multi-column key, or on some other ordinary column instead of the key, that fact gets copied onto every row sharing that value - and one edit can leave two rows disagreeing. First normal form breaks up a cell holding more than one value. Second normal form moves a column that depends on only part of the key into its own table, keyed by that part. Third normal form moves a column that depends on another ordinary column into a table of its own. Each step removes one way rows could drift apart.

blocks.caption: Drill's name is typed twice. Rename it and you'd have to catch both rows.

steps.say: Every column above is supposed to depend on both parts of this key together.
Name and price only need product_id, so copying them per order risks two rows disagreeing.
Giving products its own key means a price fix lands in exactly one row.
order_lines keeps only facts about the order, linked back through product_id.

blocks.caption: One split, and the update problem disappears.

blocks.prompt: A table enrollments(student_id, course_id, student_email, grade) is keyed on (student_id, course_id). student_email only depends on student_id. Which fix removes the risk of two rows disagreeing about the same student's email?
options: Add a unique constraint on student_email.
Move student_email into a students table keyed on student_id alone.
Add student_email to the primary key alongside student_id and course_id.
why: Uniqueness stops duplicate emails, but the same email would still be retyped on every enrollment row.
Right. student_id alone identifies the student, so email belongs in its own table keyed on just that.
That makes the key even wider without fixing why the same email keeps getting copied per course.
blocks.hint: Ask what student_email is really about - a fact about the student, or about the enrollment?
blocks.explain: student_email depends only on student_id, not on course_id, so it is a partial dependency on part of the key. Moving it into a table keyed on student_id alone stores each student's email exactly once.

blocks.prompt: A table bookings(booking_id, room_id, room_type, nightly_rate, guest_name) is keyed on booking_id alone, but room_type and nightly_rate only depend on room_id. Write one query that returns the rows a separate rooms table should hold: one row per room_id, with columns room_id, room_type, nightly_rate, ordered by room_id ascending.

tests.name: example

blocks.referenceSolution:
create table bookings(
  booking_id integer primary key,
  room_id integer,
  room_type text,
  nightly_rate numeric,
  guest_name text
);
insert into bookings values
  (1,101,'Standard',120,'Huda'),
  (2,102,'Suite',250,'Omar'),
  (3,101,'Standard',120,'Layla');

select distinct room_id, room_type, nightly_rate
from bookings
order by room_id;
blocks.hint: Which two columns are duplicated across bookings that share the same room_id?
blocks.explain: room_type and nightly_rate depend only on room_id, not on booking_id, so distinct room_id, room_type, nightly_rate pulls out exactly the rows a rooms table should hold - one per room.

bullets: Ask what each column actually depends on, not just its table.
Move a column to the table its value truly belongs to.
Each split removes one way rows could disagree after an edit.
blocks.remember: The key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.

blocks.say: New tables, new dependencies to hunt down - time to split one yourself.

lessons.exitLine: That's the split. Go find the next one.
